Phase 08 · 18–30 hours over 6 weeks

Independent practice.

Move from isolated successes to a series that asks a question. Build a repeatable cycle of research, constraint, variation, critique, selection, and revision.

Frame your questionOpen the capstone

Aim

Become your own next teacher.

Prerequisite

A portfolio with one artifact and one process record from every prior phase, plus evidence of joining, surface testing, firing literacy, and diagnosis.

By the end

You can frame a productive inquiry, develop variations, seek critique, select rigorously, and design your next learning cycle.

Deliverables

A precedent map, constraint brief, maquettes, 3–5 resolved works, process archive, critique record, and six-week plan.

08.1

A series is a controlled conversation.

What can remain constant so that one meaningful difference becomes visible?

Series logic

Constant + variable + question

Hold a family resemblance—method, scale, clay, profile logic, or surface rule—while changing one high-value variable. The contrast makes learning and meaning legible.

A useful question makes objects necessary

“How does an opening shift from invitation to refusal?” is more generative than “make organic pots.” It names a relation you can test through form.

Precedent triangulation

Study three sources: one historical work, one contemporary practitioner, and one source outside ceramics. For each, record the problem addressed, formal strategy, material consequence, and what you will not copy.

Research ethically.Credit makers and cultures precisely. Distinguish learning a general process from reproducing a distinctive contemporary work, sacred form, or culturally specific design.
Exercise · Constraint stack75 min

Write one constraint in each category: method, scale, profile, surface, function/context, and time. Remove two. The remaining four should focus the work without deciding it in advance.

Finish this sentence: “Across this series I will hold ___ constant and vary ___ to investigate ___.”

08.2

Variation is a research method.

Studio · Maquettes + variation ladder3–5 hours
  1. Make eight palm-size maquettes quickly under the same constraint stack.
  2. Arrange them by the variable you chose—least to most open, tense, asymmetric, elevated, or dense.
  3. Select three nonadjacent positions: one restrained, one threshold, one extreme.
  4. Scale those three up as studies. Record what changes because of gravity, hand reach, drying, or joining.
  5. Choose the next variation based on evidence, not attachment to the first idea.
Stop ruleIf three objects repeat the same answer, change the variable or sharpen the question. More objects do not automatically mean more inquiry.
08.3

Critique the work you made.

Describe

What is physically present? Avoid praise, dislike, and intention.

Analyze

How do form, surface, scale, and relation guide use and attention?

Propose

What single change would most strongly test the stated question?

Protocol · Evidence-first critique45 min per round
  1. Display work without explaining it. Ask viewers to write three observations and one question.
  2. Share your inquiry statement only after the first observation round.
  3. Sort feedback into: confirms intention, reveals unintended reading, execution issue, and new possibility.
  4. Choose one revision because it advances the question. Record why other suggestions were declined.

Selection test

08.4

Capstone: a resolved series.

3–5 finished works · six-week cycle

Ask one question well.

Produce a coherent series that combines structural control, meaningful variation, tested surface, documented firing, and independent diagnosis.

Pre-build feasibility gate:confirm with your studio that clay, surfaces, firing range, dimensions, thickness, and hollow-form venting are compatible. Fire the selected surface on the actual clay in the intended firing. Name the largest technical risk, run a small test, and confirm the studio calendar. Unsafe or kiln-incompatible work cannot pass.
WeekFocusEvidence
1Question, precedents, constraintsInquiry statement + source map
2Maquettes and material testsEight variations + test matrix
3First resolved works and final makingBuild logs + photographs
4Critique and revisionFeedback map + priority change
5Drying and firing already-dry workFiring and location records
6Selection and documentation3–5 works + reflection
The calendar is elastic.Clay state, thickness and geometry, test results, and studio kiln access—not a week number—control progression. Never use concentrated heat or submit internally damp work to meet the plan.

Final documentation

  1. Photograph each work alone and the series together: front, side, top, detail, and scale/use view.
  2. Include clay, methods, dimensions, surface materials, firing, date, and image credits.
  3. Write 250–400 words—or record a 5–7 minute reflection with an outline—covering the question, constants, variable, pivotal evidence, feedback accepted and declined, precedents transformed and deliberately not borrowed, the least necessary work, a flaw preserved versus corrected, unresolved uncertainty, an alternative explanation, and the next test.
  4. Create a one-page process map linking at least three decisions to evidence.

Course evidence map

For each phase, record the competency, artifact, process record, diagnosis or decision, present level, and next need. Use the shared scale: 0 no evidence; 1 recognition; 2 guided performance; 3 independent competence; 4 adaptive competence. Summarize four domains: understanding, execution, judgment, and reflection/transfer.

Inspiration · look comparatively

Ceramic languages can change what the medium does.

Compare a vessel that performs sound and narrative, an amphora where figure and ground choreograph one another, and a platter transformed into topography.

Knowledge check · 3 questions

Pause. Predict. Diagnose.

Choose one answer for each situation. Open a hint when needed; explanations appear after you check all three.

Capstone review · 32 points

Can you sustain an independent learning cycle?

Criterion1234
InquiryTheme onlyBroad questionQuestion drives choicesObjects deepen the question
Series logicUnrelated worksVisual similarityClear constants/variableEach work adds a distinct answer
Form/function/encounterUnsafe or unresolvedPartly worksIntended encounter worksUse and meaning reinforce each other
Surface–form integrationAfterthoughtLoosely relatedSurface responds to volumeSurface and form are inseparable
Technical controlFailures obscure workUnevenMethods support intentRisk is controlled and purposeful
Evidence/revisionNo trailDocuments activityEvidence changes decisionsTests separate competing choices
Context/ethicsSources absentSources namedInfluence analyzed and creditedPrinciples transformed independently
Self-directionWaits for answersPlans next taskNames gap and next testBuilds a sustainable learning plan
Capstone standard: 24/32 with no criterion below 2.Functional work must also pass relevant stability, grip/lift, pour or lid, cleaning, edge, integrity, and studio material-use checks. Unsafe or kiln-incompatible work cannot pass. A lower score identifies the small cycle to repeat.

Your next six weeks

Schedule one narrow question and one evidence-based bottleneck; one focused drill repeated at least four times; one small integrated project; one controlled comparison; one named feedback source and date; a weekly retrieval/reflection routine; and a decision date for reviewing evidence and choosing the next cycle. Independence is not working alone—it is knowing when and how to seek useful evidence.

Course-wide exit prompts
  1. Explain how water, force, time, geometry, and heat interact across the whole process.
  2. Show one example where a test changed your making decision.
  3. Diagnose one unfamiliar defect using event × location × evidence.
  4. Name your strongest skill, most consequential gap, and next deliberate-practice exercise.
